solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Fantastic beat in chorus

indicators.note: one word is placed inside the word for a chorus, held within it

blocks.note: a chorus is a group that sings together
to beat food to a pulp is to mash it

explanation.surface: A singer praises a wonderful rhythm heard in the chorus of a song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beat' reads as a musical rhythm, but it is the verb meaning crush, sitting inside the singing.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are informal British praise for something excellent or wonderful.

clue.text: Small rescue vessel needed for small island

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small
Noah's ark rescued the animals from the Flood

explanation.surface: A little lifeboat is required to reach a tiny island.
explanation.definitionFit: Sark is one of the smaller Channel Islands, lying between Guernsey and Jersey.

clue.text: Aiming to get rid of good drug

indicators.note: getting rid of something removes it, so a letter is taken out

blocks.note: aspiring to something is aiming at it
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: Someone is trying to give up a beneficial medicine.
explanation.definitionFit: Aspirin is a common painkilling drug, acetylsalicylic acid.

clue.text: Playboy in robbery framing mafia boss

indicators.note: a frame surrounds a picture, so one word goes around the other

blocks.note: a heist is a robbery
a Mafia boss is called a don

explanation.surface: A playboy gets caught up in a robbery that frames a Mafia chief.
explanation.definitionFit: A playboy lives for pleasure, and a hedonist is a pleasure-seeker.

clue.text: Shameful reason for changing full-on approach

indicators.note: changing the letters means they are rearranged into a different order

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange, taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone has a disgraceful motive for altering an all-out strategy.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes doing something thoroughly and wholeheartedly, without compromise.

clue.text: Makes incisions around firm plaster

indicators.note: turned around, the word for making incisions is read from its end back to its start

blocks.note: someone who makes incisions cuts
CO is the abbreviation for company, a firm

explanation.surface: A plasterer scores a surface before applying a firm coat of plaster.
explanation.definitionFit: Stucco is a fine plaster used to coat walls or make mouldings.

clue.text: Pilot restrains British family

definitions.note: family is used attributively, as in family loyalty, matching the adjective

indicators.note: to restrain is to hold in, so one letter is held inside the other word

blocks.note: a pilot scheme is a trial run
B is the abbreviation for British

explanation.surface: An airline pilot holds back a British family.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pilot' is not a flier but the adjective-noun for a test run.
explanation.definitionFit: Tribal means relating to a tribe or clan, a kinship group like a family.

clue.text: Cup of tea left on rocks

blocks.note: cha, or char, is British slang for tea
L is the abbreviation for left
a drink on the rocks is served over ice

explanation.surface: A cup of tea has been abandoned on some rocks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the rocks' is bar talk for served with ice.
explanation.definitionFit: A chalice is a goblet or ceremonial drinking cup, as used for Communion wine.

clue.text: Doctor has to operate in huge Kent properties

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so its letters are altered
one word is placed inside the abbreviation that follows

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange, taken as written
OS is the clothing-size abbreviation for outsize
to operate a machine is to use it

explanation.surface: A medic must work in enormous houses in Kent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To' does double duty: it is part of the anagram letters. Oast houses are buildings for drying hops, a famous sight in the county of Kent in south-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: Oast houses, with their conical roofs, are buildings associated above all with Kent's hop farms.

clue.text: Ready to trade on A1?

blocks.note: surface and plain reading: readies, that is money, available for a business to trade with
setter's reading: A is a capital letter, and A1 means in good order, so a capital that is functioning

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ready' is British slang for cash; A1 also suggests the road to London, a capital, which adds to the misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: This accounting term means the liquid funds a business has available for its day-to-day operations.

clue.text: Fleet‘s pressure in attack

indicators.note: one letter sits inside the word for an attack, held within it

blocks.note: a raid is a sudden attack
P is the physics symbol for pressure

explanation.surface: A naval fleet comes under pressure during an attack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fleet' looks like a noun for ships, but here it is the adjective meaning swift.
explanation.definitionFit: Fleet as an adjective means fast-moving or swift, a synonym of quick.

clue.text: More than one tough problem I see over hotel backing

definitions.note: tough is used as a noun meaning a thug, so this is a plural noun

indicators.note: backing means moving backwards, so the whole string is read from right to left

blocks.note: a snag is a small problem
taken as written
lo is an old word for look or see
O is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for an over
Hotel is the NATO alphabet word for H

explanation.surface: A traveller reports a hard problem with the hotel's support.
explanation.walkthrough: A tough, as a noun, is a rough violent man; 'more than one' makes it plural.
explanation.definitionFit: Hooligans are rowdy, violent troublemakers, just as toughs are thuggish men.

clue.text: Quaff many pints of Bass?

blocks.note: surface reading: drinking a lot of Bass, a well-known English brand of beer
setter's reading: a bass is also a fish, so the drinking is done in the manner of a fish

explanation.walkthrough: Bass is a British beer brand as well as a sea fish; the idiom describes heavy drinking, and the question mark flags the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to drink alcohol heavily and habitually, as a fish seemingly gulps water.

clue.text: In one capital city, US base

blocks.note: taken as written
I is the Roman numeral for one
Quito is the capital of Ecuador
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sentence about an American military base in some capital city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Base' looks like a military post; it is the adjective meaning low and immoral.
explanation.definitionFit: Base as an adjective means morally low, and iniquitous means grossly wicked or unjust.

clue.text: Singer at home while I’m cutting new single

indicators.note: to cut into something is to go into its middle, splitting it apart

blocks.note: someone at home is in
as can mean while, during the time that
taken as written, apostrophe dropped
N is the abbreviation for new
single means one

explanation.surface: A musician at home announces she is recording a new single.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cutting' sounds like recording a disc, but it means splitting the last two pieces apart to take the first three.
explanation.definitionFit: Nina Simone was an American jazz and soul singer and pianist.

clue.text: One loving the sound of a violin player?

indicators.note: the sound of tells us only how a word is said matters, not its spelling

blocks.note: a violin is played with a bow, which is said the same as this French-derived word

explanation.surface: Someone loves listening to a violinist.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'player' is not the violinist but the bow drawn across the strings.
explanation.definitionFit: A beau is a boyfriend or admirer, someone in love with another person.

clue.text: Leaving motorway premises drunk, getting very strong coffee

indicators.note: what is left behind departs, so those letters are taken away
something drunk staggers about, so its letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the M1 is Britain's main north-south motorway, with 1 read as I
taken as written before the deletion
so can mean very, as in so tired

explanation.surface: Someone stumbles out of a pub by the motorway and orders a strong coffee.
explanation.walkthrough: M and I are taken from the letters of premises; the M1 is the motorway from London to Leeds.
explanation.definitionFit: An espresso is a small, strong black coffee made by forcing steam through ground beans.

clue.text: Left somewhat short

indicators.note: a word that is short has lost its final letter

blocks.note: somewhat means quite, fairly

explanation.surface: Someone departed rather briefly.
explanation.definitionFit: To quit a place is to leave it, so quit in the past tense means departed.

clue.text: I caught diver’s upturned frozen body

indicators.note: in a down clue, turned up means the word is read from bottom to top

blocks.note: taken as written
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
a grebe is a diving water bird

explanation.surface: Someone catches sight of a diver's capsized, frozen corpse.
explanation.walkthrough: The diver is a bird, not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: An iceberg is a large floating mass of frozen ice broken off a glacier.

clue.text: Old Italian ready to eat a new bread for cheese

indicators.note: what eats something takes it inside, so one piece swallows the others

blocks.note: the lira was Italy's money before the euro; ready, or readies, is slang for cash
taken as written
N is the abbreviation for new
bread is slang for money

explanation.surface: An old Italian, ready for dinner, eats new bread with cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ready' and 'bread' both look like food talk but are money slang; the lira was Italy's currency before the euro.
explanation.definitionFit: Lancashire is a crumbly English cheese named after the north-western county.

clue.text: Maroon tie, also pants

indicators.note: pants is British slang for rubbish, so the letters are a poor arrangement to be fixed

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange, taken as written

explanation.surface: A dark red tie, and some trousers too.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maroon' looks like a colour but is the verb meaning strand; British pants are underwear, and 'pants' is also slang for bad.
explanation.definitionFit: To maroon someone is to abandon them alone, as on a desert island, cutting them off.

clue.text: Good acting parts see you getting past

indicators.note: to part something is to split it, so other letters go into the gap

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for good
an actor on stage is on
see you is a casual goodbye

explanation.surface: Fine stage roles say farewell as one grows older.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parts' looks like stage roles, but it is the verb meaning splits.
explanation.definitionFit: Bygone means belonging to an earlier time, long gone and in the past.

clue.text: Forgive me for what?

blocks.note: first meaning: a polite apology
second meaning: a request to repeat something not heard

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a puzzled question about what one is being forgiven for; in fact both halves are uses of one phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase serves both as an apology and as a request to repeat something unheard.

clue.text: Benefit of luxury slightly reduced

indicators.note: reduced by just a little means only the final letter is cut off

blocks.note: plush means luxurious, or a luxurious fabric

explanation.surface: The perks of a luxury lifestyle have been trimmed a little.
explanation.definitionFit: A plus is an advantage or positive point, a synonym of benefit.

clue.text: Please hold books about captain and crew

indicators.note: the books go round the outside of the other pieces, enclosing them

blocks.note: OT is the Old Testament, a set of books of the Bible
Captain Nemo commands the Nautilus in Jules Verne's novels
a ship's crew are its men

explanation.surface: A request to wait while books on a captain and his crew are fetched.
explanation.walkthrough: The captain is Jules Verne's, not a generic ship's master; the crew are simply men.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are what a receptionist says when asking a caller to wait briefly on the line.

clue.text: Enclosure made by hedge

blocks.note: first meaning: a compartment for an animal in a stable
second meaning: to evade or play for time

explanation.surface: A pen fenced in by a row of bushes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hedge' looks like the garden boundary but is the verb meaning to avoid committing.
explanation.definitionFit: A stall is a pen in a barn, and to stall is to delay or evade, as one hedges.

clue.text: Retreating soldiers capture seal

indicators.note: retreating troops move backwards, so their word is read from end to start

blocks.note: GIs are American soldiers
to net something is to catch or capture it

explanation.surface: Withdrawing troops seize a marine animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seal' suggests the animal, but it is the stamp pressed into wax.
explanation.definitionFit: A signet is a small seal, often set in a ring, used to authenticate documents.

clue.text: Underwear for boobs

blocks.note: first meaning: baggy knee-length knickers
second meaning: blunders, mistakes

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a bra; 'boobs' is in fact a plural noun meaning gaffes.
explanation.definitionFit: Bloomers are loose women's knickers, and a bloomer is also a silly mistake or blunder.
